analysis.one_liner: Stops the Labor Department from raising the wage floor it sets for temporary foreign guestworkers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 29 House Republicans, was referred to the Judiciary Committee, sent to an immigration subcommittee on October 24, 2011, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Labor Department had written a rule that would raise the minimum wage employers must pay H-2B temporary foreign workers — people brought in for seasonal jobs like landscaping, seafood processing, and hospitality. This bill would forbid the Labor Department from putting that wage rule into effect, and would also bar a related proposed rule expanding the program's protections. It would instead require the Department to use a different, lower-cost wage data source for certain skilled-worker certifications.
analysis.who_benefits: Seasonal employers who use H-2B guestworkers — landscaping companies, seafood processors, hotels, and forestry contractors — would avoid paying the higher wage the Labor Department rule would have required, keeping their labor costs down. Staffing and recruiting agencies that place guestworkers, and universities and nonprofit research organizations affected by the certification wage calculation, would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids the Secretary of Labor from implementing, amending, or enforcing the January 2011 rule 'Wage Methodology for the Temporary Non-agricultural Employment H-2B Program,' which recalculated the prevailing wage H-2B employers must pay, and from finalizing or enforcing a related proposed rule on H-2B employment [S2] [S3].

It directs the Secretary to use Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment Statistics data, with a set number of wage levels, when computing prevailing wages for labor certifications used by institutions of higher education and nonprofit research organizations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: H-2B guestworkers would forgo the higher wage floor the rule was meant to provide, and U.S. workers in the same seasonal occupations — for whom the prevailing-wage rule also acts as a wage floor — would forgo the wage protection it contained. The costs are borne entirely by the workers the rule was designed to cover.

drawbacks.text: The bill takes away the Labor Department's authority to set wage methodology for the H-2B program by naming specific rules the Secretary may not enforce, locking in the lower wage structure employers were already using [S2] [S3].

Employers' strongest argument for the bill is that the wage rule would significantly raise costs for small seasonal businesses, potentially leading them to hire fewer workers or cut positions; an honest supporter would acknowledge that this cost relief comes at the price of lower wages for the guestworkers and U.S. workers in those jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits of this bill flow almost entirely to seasonal employers who save on labor costs; the costs fall on guestworkers and U.S. workers who would have received a higher wage floor. The prevailing-wage rule exists precisely to prevent guestworker hiring from pulling down wages in seasonal trades, so blocking it shifts the balance squarely toward employers. There is no provision offsetting the wage loss to workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its immigration subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rodney Alexander introduced the bill on October 12, 2011, with 28 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on October 24, 2011, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Immigration Policy and Enforcement [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote in either chamber — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, no law blocked the Labor Department's guestworker wage rules, so the workers those rules cover were spared the wage cut this bill would have frozen in. The outcome left the matter where it already stood, rather than handing seasonal employers the savings the bill promised.

for.name: 28 of 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 28 were Republicans.

for.name: Reps. Wittman, Harris, and Boustany
for.role: Original cosponsors from Virginia, Maryland, and Louisiana
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors at introduction, from districts with large seasonal-employer industries.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Referral committee; its chair never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 12, 2011, and sent it to the Subcommittee on Immigration Policy and Enforcement on October 24, 2011, where it stayed without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 28 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, though it never advanced far enough for a vote to test the rest of the chamber.

industries.industry: Seasonal H-2B employers (landscaping, seafood processing, hospitality, forestry)
industries.note: The bill would let these employers avoid the higher prevailing wage the Labor Department rule required, cutting their largest seasonal cost. Their gain comes directly out of the wages of guestworkers and U.S. workers in the same jobs.

Agencies that recruit and place guestworkers benefit because lower wage requirements make the program cheaper to use and easier to sell to employers. Their profit depends on the wage gap the bill would preserve.

The bill mandates a specific wage-data method for their worker certifications, which could lower certification wage figures and simplify compliance. This is a narrow administrative change with modest stakes for most workers.
